1: # Wiki Schema & Workflow
2: 
3: Conventions for maintaining EDAC's wiki — SystemBuilder's research/verification
4: knowledge base. This file is the contract every wiki actor follows: SystemBuilder

7: > ## EDAC ↔ OAC relationship (read first)
8: > EDAC is **inspired by** OpenAgentsControl (OAC) but has **no obligation to follow OAC specifics** — especially the structure of the local `.opencode/`.
9: > - OAC patterns, where they exist, live **exclusively in `src/`**.
10: > - For the purposes of EDAC: **OAC ≈ `src/`**.
11: > - `src/` is a **focused derivation and enhancement** of OAC, not a mirror.
12: >
13: > Consequence for the wiki: pages derived from OAC sources describe OAC *lineage* and are generalized, not authoritative EDAC layout. Treat `src/` as the source of truth for EDAC structure (see [framework/src-structure.md](framework/src-structure.md)). Do **not** assume OAC directory layouts, file names, or metadata locations apply to EDAC's `.opencode/`.
14: 
15: ## Purpose
16: The wiki is a persistent, compounding knowledge base used while developing `src/`.
17: It is not a user-facing browse tool. The user interacts only with SystemBuilder;
18: subagents are spawned by SystemBuilder, never directly.

20: Pattern reference: `llm-wiki.md` (the abstract LLM-wiki idea this repo instantiates).

22: ## Layout
23: - `sources/` — raw, immutable primary data. ResearchAgent writes cited research docs here; the user may also drop sources. Never modified after creation.
24: - `framework/` — generated pages on EDAC's conceptual architecture (agentic-system design, the layered model, registry/install model, component taxonomy).
25: - `harness/` — generated pages on OpenCode harness specifics (agent frontmatter, permission model, tools, MCP, subagent spawning, context/`compress`).
26: - `research/` — generated pages on external references, findings, comparisons (OpenAgentsControl lineage, upstream OpenCode docs, related projects).
27: - `SCHEMA.md` — this file.
28: - `index.md` — content catalog (updated every ingest).
29: - `log.md` — chronological activity record (append-only).
30: - `TODO.md` — cross-session build plan for the wiki workflow itself.

32: ## Page format
33: Every generated page (under `framework/` `harness/` `research/`) starts with YAML frontmatter:
34: 
35: ```yaml
36: ---
37: title: Short page title
38: type: entity | concept | comparison | summary | source-note
39: tags: [comma, separated]
40: created: YYYY-MM-DD
41: updated: YYYY-MM-DD
42: sources: [sources/stub.md, https://...]
43: status: draft | stable
44: ---
45: ```
46: 
47: Body: markdown. Lead with the finding, then evidence. Cross-link to sibling pages with relative links (`../harness/permissions.md`). Note contradictions explicitly rather than silently overwriting.
48: 
49: ## Source format (in `sources/`)
50: One file per research stub, named `lower-case-stub.md`. Frontmatter:
51: 
52: ```yaml
53: ---
54: title: Source title
55: url: https://...   # or "local" if user-dropped
56: retrieved: YYYY-MM-DD
57: author: ...
58: ---
59: ```
60: 
61: Body: structured notes + verbatim quotes where useful, with inline citations. ResearchAgent works in `.tmp/{stub}/external-research/` and writes the final cited doc to `sources/{stub}.md`.
62: 
63: ## Procedures
64: ### Research (ResearchAgent)
65: Gather external data via web search / fetch / curl / wget. Produce a structured, cited doc in `sources/`. Scratch work stays in `.tmp/{stub}/external-research/` and is not committed.
66: 
67: ### Ingest (WikiJanitor)
68: Given a source, create/update relevant pages across `framework/` `harness/` `research/`, add cross-references, then update `index.md` and append to `log.md`. A single source may touch many pages.
69: 
70: ### Query (WikiLibrarian)
71: Read `index.md` to locate relevant pages, read them, synthesize an answer with citations. Good answers may be filed back as new pages.
72: 
73: ### Lint (WikiJanitor)
74: Run after every ingest and on demand. Scope: only generated pages under `framework/`, `harness/`, `research/`. WikiJanitor may use **read-only** git (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git ls-files`, `git rev-parse`) to inspect repo state for verification, but never commits, pushes, or modifies the working tree.
75: 
76: > **`sources/` is immutable OAC raw documentation — never lint it for OAC paths; those are upstream documents, not EDAC assertions.** Correction/explanation contexts (`wiki/TODO.md`, `wiki/log.md`, `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`) are exempt from the OAC-path checks below because they deliberately quote the wrong forms to explain the fix.

78: **1. OAC-path tyranny** — no generated page may assert an OAC `.opencode/` path or a wrong `src/` path as EDAC fact. The greps below must return **zero matches** (Lint passes when grep fails). Run from `wiki/`:

87: 
88: # 1c. registry.json lives at repo root, never under src/

90: ```
91: 
92: 1d. **Structural-claim traceability** — every EDAC file path, directory, or layout assertion in a generated page must trace to `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`. For each path-like token a page asserts, confirm it appears in (or is consistent with) the tables in `src-structure.md`. If a claim cannot be traced, correct it against the live `src/` tree or flag it in `TODO.md`.
93: 
94: **2. Cross-link integrity**
95: - Every relative markdown link (`[text](path.md)`, `[text](../dir/page.md)`) must resolve to an existing file. Extract links, then verify each target exists relative to the referencing page:
96:   ```bash
97:   rg -no '\[[^\]]+\]\(([^)]+\.md)\)' framework harness research
98:   ```
99:   (Anchored links `path.md#sec` are rare here; re-check any that the pattern misses.)
100: - **Orphan pages** — flag any generated page with zero inbound links (no other page links to it). Cross-check against `index.md` and the link graph.
101: - **Missing pages** — flag concepts/entities named in pages (especially `tags`, `sources`, and "Related" sections) that are referenced but have no corresponding page.
102: 
103: **3. Frontmatter compliance** — every generated page must open with valid YAML frontmatter containing exactly these keys: `title`, `type`, `tags`, `created`, `updated`, `sources`, `status`. Verify:
104: ```bash
105: for f in $(rg -l '^---$' framework harness research); do
106:   rg -q '^title:' "$f" && rg -q '^type:' "$f" && rg -q '^tags:' "$f" \
107:     && rg -q '^created:' "$f" && rg -q '^updated:' "$f" \
108:     && rg -q '^sources:' "$f" && rg -q '^status:' "$f" || echo "MISSING FRONTMATTER KEY: $f"
109: done
110: ```
111: Also confirm `type` ∈ {entity, concept, comparison, summary, source-note} and `status` ∈ {draft, stable} per the Page format section.
112: 
113: **4. Contradictions** — pages must not contradict each other, nor contradict `wiki/framework/src-structure.md` or the actual `src/` tree. Reconcile any conflicting claims (differing paths, component lists, version facts) by re-reading `src-structure.md` and the live `src/` directory; record resolutions in `log.md` and fix the offending page. Note contradictions explicitly rather than silently overwriting (per Page format).
114: 
115: **5. Stale claims** — verify version/file assertions against the repo. Confirm these exist at the stated locations (paths relative to `wiki/`):
116: ```bash
117: test -f ../VERSION && echo "VERSION ok" || echo "MISSING: ../VERSION"
118: test -f ../package.json && echo "package.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../package.json"
119: test -f ../registry.json && echo "registry.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../registry.json"
120: test -f ../src/metadata.json && echo "src/metadata.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../src/metadata.json"
121: ```
122: Any page asserting a version, file, or path that does not match the live repo is stale and must be corrected.
123: 
124: **6. Secret scan** — WikiJanitor may `grep` *any* directory (its `grep` permission is intentionally broad) to detect leaked secrets — API keys, tokens, credentials — that have landed in normal files. Sensitive-file paths (`.env`, `.key`, `.secret`, `.pem`, `.crt`, `credentials*`) are denied under `grep`, so known-secret files are never opened; only leaks into ordinary files are surfaced. Flag leaks to SystemBuilder; never write secret values into wiki pages.
125: 
126: ### Cross-Reference Protocol
127: The wiki must be a navigable graph, not a set of standalone blobs. Every page is responsible for linking its related concepts inline so WikiLibrarian can traverse and Lint can verify.
128: 
129: - **Inline links are mandatory.** Whenever a page mentions a concept that has (or should have) its own wiki page, embed an inline markdown link in the prose — e.g. `the [permission model](./permission-model.md) governs access`. A trailing `## Related` section is a supplement only; it does **not** substitute for inline links. Inline links are grep-discoverable, which is what Lint checks (Check 2) and what lets WikiLibrarian walk the graph.
130: - **Back-links.** When page A links to page B, WikiJanitor also ensures B's `## Related` (and, where natural, B's prose) acknowledges A — unless B is a deliberate hub. This keeps the graph bidirectional.
131: - **Lint enforces** (Check 2): inline + `## Related` links resolve; no orphan page (zero inbound links); gap detection — a concept mentioned but lacking a page is a candidate for the ingest queue (fed to ResearchAgent / WikiLibrarian); bidirectional-consistency warning on asymmetry (asymmetry is allowed for hubs, so warn, don't fail).
132: - **Format.** Use relative markdown links to the target `.md` (`[label](./target.md)` or `[label](../dir/target.md)`). Keep the label human-readable; the link target is what Lint greps.
133: 
134: ## index.md format
135: Catalog of all pages, grouped by directory, each with a one-line summary and optional metadata (date, source count). Updated on every ingest. Example:
136: 
137: ```markdown
138: # Wiki Index
139: ## framework/
140: - [Layered Architecture](framework/layered-architecture.md) — the 6-layer model.
141: ## harness/
142: - [Permission Model](harness/permission-model.md) — frontmatter allow/deny/ask.
143: ```
144: 
145: ## log.md format
146: Append-only. Each entry begins with a consistent prefix so it is parseable:
147: `## [YYYY-MM-DD] <op> | <Title>` where `<op>` ∈ `init | research | ingest | query | lint`. Example:
148: `## [2026-07-29] init | Wiki scaffolding created`.
149: 
150: ## Workflow is branching
151: The research loop is not a fixed sequence. SystemBuilder may fan out multiple subagents in parallel (e.g. several ResearchAgents, several WikiLibrarians) and may spawn itself (configured `mode: all`). WikiJanitor's ingest runs only when new research was produced; if a query is answered from existing pages, no research/ingest occurs.

I've oriented against the governing schema, the WikiJanitor definition, and the current wiki layout. Here's my read of the request and a proposed design — **not yet built**, per your "Suggest."

## Intent (restated)
You want a **low-friction capture buffer** in `wiki/` where, mid-task, you (or I) can drop a one-line note about a wiki flaw and immediately return to the real work. WikiJanitor later drains that buffer — triaging, fixing mechanical issues, or promoting/escalating the rest. The design goal is *non-derailment*: capture must be cheaper than the correction it defers.

## Proposed architecture

**AUDIT.md = an ephemeral, append-style capture buffer** — distinct from `TODO.md` (the curated build plan) and `log.md` (the append-only activity record). Pipeline:

```
mid-task flaw found ──► AUDIT.md (## Open, one bullet each)
                              │
                    WikiJanitor "Audit" drain
                              ├─ mechanical fix  ──► fix page + log.md entry + move bullet to ## Resolved
                              ├─ planned work    ──► promote to TODO.md + move bullet to ## Resolved
                              └─ semantic/unverifiable ──► escalate to SystemBuilder + move bullet to ## Resolved
```

The `## Open` section is WikiJanitor's idempotent work queue; `## Resolved` preserves a trail so the buffer stays bounded and draining is repeatable.

**Schema changes (SCHEMA.md):**
- **Layout** — add `AUDIT.md` with a one-line description (fast-capture buffer; drained by WikiJanitor).
- **Procedures** — add two sub-procedures: *Audit capture* (who writes, format) and *Audit drain (WikiJanitor)* (triage rules, lifecycle, log/TODO hand-off).
- **Lint exemptions** — add `AUDIT.md` to the list of files exempt from the generated-page checks (frontmatter, OAC-path, cross-link), since it is not a generated page. (It already sits beside `SCHEMA.md`/`TODO.md`/`log.md` in that exemption class.)

**WikiJanitor changes (`.opencode/agents/subagents/wiki-janitor.md`):**
- Add a **Tier 3 "Audit"** procedure: read `AUDIT.md` `## Open`, triage each bullet, fix mechanical issues, promote planned work to `TODO.md`, escalate semantic to SystemBuilder, append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] audit | <title>` to `log.md`, move processed bullets to `## Resolved`.
- No frontmatter `permission` change needed — `edit: "wiki/**": "allow"` and `read: "wiki/**": "allow"` already cover `AUDIT.md`.
- Keep Lint (Tier 2) scoped to generated pages; AUDIT.md is explicitly excluded there (mirrors the SCHEMA exemption).

## The forks (genuine decisions — your call)

1. **Capture format — friction vs. parseability.**
   - *A1 (recommended):* minimal bullet `- [YYYY-MM-DD] <where>: <flaw>`; `where`/`severity`/`fix` optional free text. WikiJanitor (LLM) parses it. Lowest friction, matches "make a note and move on."
   - *A2:* structured block with optional fields (`Where` / `Flaw` / `Fix` / `Severity`). More reliable draining, slightly more to type.
   - I recommend **A1** — the whole point is non-derailment; a bullet is faster than the correction it replaces.

2. **Lifecycle — archive vs. delete on resolve.**
   - *B1 (recommended):* move resolved bullets to `## Resolved` (trail preserved, idempotent drain).
   - *B2:* delete on resolve (pure scratchpad, no history).
   - I recommend **B1** for traceability; B2 if you want AUDIT.md to stay a true scratchpad.

3. **Drain trigger.**
   - *C1 (recommended):* dedicated Audit tier, invoked ad-hoc by me or on a heuristic (e.g. Open-count threshold / session boundary).
   - *C2:* fold drain into the existing Lint tier as a pre-step.
   - I recommend **C1** — keeps Lint scoped to generated pages and preserves the separation of concerns already in the schema.

4. **Scope of captured flaws.**
   - You said "a flaw in the wiki" — I'll scope AUDIT.md to **wiki flaws only**. (Generalizing to `src/` flaws is a natural extension; I'll leave it out unless you want it.)

## Scope boundary (what I will *not* do without separate approval)
- I will **not** edit `AGENTS.md` (it mentions wiki conventions; updating it is an adjacent improvement, not part of this request).
- I will **not** build anything yet — this is the proposal. I'll implement only after you approve the forks.
- I will **not** pre-populate AUDIT.md with the existing `TODO.md` "Lint findings" (those are already curated; migrating them is a separate decision).

**How would you like me to resolve forks 1–4, and shall I proceed to build once set?** My defaults: A1, B1, C1, wiki-scoped.

Agreed — and your instinct is the cleaner architecture. Audit has no business in Ingest: Ingest has a single focused input (a source) and a single output (pages); mixing in unrelated audit bullets would fracture its context. Audit is a *verification* act, which is exactly what Lint already is. So fold it into Lint — but as a **bounded prefix**, not a third tier.

## Proposed design

**Ingest (Tier 1) — untouched, audit-free.**
Its post-ingest lint stays scoped to *changed pages only* and never reads `AUDIT.md`. This honours your "ingest not derailed" requirement at the structural level.

**Lint (Tier 2) — gains a Step 0 "Audit drain," standalone invocations only.**
When WikiJanitor is invoked for a *standalone* Lint (by WikiLibrarian or me), it runs, *before* the six checks:
1. Read `AUDIT.md` bullets.
2. For each (bounded — see Fork Y): **verify the problem** and **verify the proposed fix** against `src/` or `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`.
3. Both verify → apply fix, append `## [date] audit | <title>` to `log.md`, **delete the bullet**.
4. Either fails → **escalate to SystemBuilder** (carry the bullet), log it, **delete the bullet**.
5. **Hard rule: no ResearchAgent spawn, no external research during audit drain** (Fork Z). Unverifiable-with-local-sources → escalate, don't investigate.
6. Then run the normal six lint checks — which naturally re-validate the just-fixed pages.

## Why this kills the tangent/time risk
- **No third tier** → no new branch; it's a linear prefix to an existing invocation.
- **No-op when empty** → when `AUDIT.md` is empty (the normal state), Step 0 costs nothing. Audit only adds latency when there are pending bullets — exactly when you want it drained. No separate scheduler/threshold needed.
- **No ResearchAgent** → the real time-explosion (spawning research subagents) is forbidden. Audit resolves only what's verifiable locally; everything else escalates.
- **Bounded cap (Fork Y)** → a run can't balloon if `AUDIT.md` somehow accumulates many bullets.
- **Delete-on-process** → idempotent; re-running Lint never double-fixes.

## Edits this implies (when we build)
- **WikiJanitor**: Tier 1 explicitly states "does not read/process `AUDIT.md`"; Tier 2 gains Step 0 (standalone Lint only) with the no-ResearchAgent poka-yoke and the cap; `conflict_resolution`/`Workflow` note audit is lint-prefixed, never ingest.
- **SCHEMA.md**: my earlier "Audit drain" wording said *"Invoked ad-hoc by SystemBuilder, or when the Open-bullet count crosses a threshold"* — that implied a separate invocation and now conflicts with this design. I'll revise it to *"runs as Step 0 of a standalone Lint invocation (never Ingest)."* The verify-then-fix / delete / escalate rules stay.

## Forks to confirm
- **X — drain trigger**: (a) *standalone Lint only* **(recommended)** vs (b) also on post-ingest lint. I strongly advise (a); (b) re-introduces audit into Ingest, which you ruled out.
- **Y — bound per run**: (a) cap at **N bullets/run** (recommend N=10) vs (b) drain all. Cap protects run length.
- **Z — research prohibition**: (a) *hard ban* on ResearchAgent during audit **(recommended)** vs (b) allow escalate-to-research. (a) is the anti-tangent guarantee.

## Scope boundary
Proposal only — I won't touch `wiki-janitor.md` or `SCHEMA.md` until you approve. `AGENTS.md` untouched.

# LLM Wiki

A pattern for building personal knowledge bases using LLMs.

This is an idea file, it is designed to be copy pasted to your own LLM Agent (e.g. OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode / Pi, or etc.). Its goal is to communicate the high level idea, but your agent will build out the specifics in collaboration with you.

## The core idea

Most people's experience with LLMs and documents looks like RAG: you upload a collection of files, the LLM retrieves relevant chunks at query time, and generates an answer. This works, but the LLM is rediscovering knowledge from scratch on every question. There's no accumulation. Ask a subtle question that requires synthesizing five documents, and the LLM has to find and piece together the relevant fragments every time. Nothing is built up. NotebookLM, ChatGPT file uploads, and most RAG systems work this way.

The idea here is different. Instead of just retrieving from raw documents at query time, the LLM **incrementally builds and maintains a persistent wiki** — a structured, interlinked collection of markdown files that sits between you and the raw sources. When you add a new source, the LLM doesn't just index it for later retrieval. It reads it, extracts the key information, and integrates it into the existing wiki — updating entity pages, revising topic summaries, noting where new data contradicts old claims, strengthening or challenging the evolving synthesis. The knowledge is compiled once and then *kept current*, not re-derived on every query.

This is the key difference: **the wiki is a persistent, compounding artifact.** The cross-references are already there. The contradictions have already been flagged. The synthesis already reflects everything you've read. The wiki keeps getting richer with every source you add and every question you ask.

You never (or rarely) write the wiki yourself — the LLM writes and maintains all of it. You're in charge of sourcing, exploration, and asking the right questions. The LLM does all the grunt work — the summarizing, cross-referencing, filing, and bookkeeping that makes a knowledge base actually useful over time. In practice, I have the LLM agent open on one side and Obsidian open on the other. The LLM makes edits based on our conversation, and I browse the results in real time — following links, checking the graph view, reading the updated pages. Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.

This can apply to a lot of different contexts. A few examples:

- **Personal**: tracking your own goals, health, psychology, self-improvement — filing journal entries, articles, podcast notes, and building up a structured picture of yourself over time.
- **Research**: going deep on a topic over weeks or months — reading papers, articles, reports, and incrementally building a comprehensive wiki with an evolving thesis.
- **Reading a book**: filing each chapter as you go, building out pages for characters, themes, plot threads, and how they connect. By the end you have a rich companion wiki. Think of fan wikis like [Tolkien Gateway](https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Main_Page) — thousands of interlinked pages covering characters, places, events, languages, built by a community of volunteers over years. You could build something like that personally as you read, with the LLM doing all the cross-referencing and maintenance.
- **Business/team**: an internal wiki maintained by LLMs, fed by Slack threads, meeting transcripts, project documents, customer calls. Possibly with humans in the loop reviewing updates. The wiki stays current because the LLM does the maintenance that no one on the team wants to do.
- **Competitive analysis, due diligence, trip planning, course notes, hobby deep-dives** — anything where you're accumulating knowledge over time and want it organized rather than scattered.

## Architecture

There are three layers:

**Raw sources** — your curated collection of source documents. Articles, papers, images, data files. These are immutable — the LLM reads from them but never modifies them. This is your source of truth.

**The wiki** — a directory of LLM-generated markdown files. Summaries, entity pages, concept pages, comparisons, an overview, a synthesis. The LLM owns this layer entirely. It creates pages, updates them when new sources arrive, maintains cross-references, and keeps everything consistent. You read it; the LLM writes it.

**The schema** — a document (e.g. CLAUDE.md for Claude Code or AGENTS.md for Codex) that tells the LLM how the wiki is structured, what the conventions are, and what workflows to follow when ingesting sources, answering questions, or maintaining the wiki. This is the key configuration file — it's what makes the LLM a disciplined wiki maintainer rather than a generic chatbot. You and the LLM co-evolve this over time as you figure out what works for your domain.

## Operations

**Ingest.** You drop a new source into the raw collection and tell the LLM to process it. An example flow: the LLM reads the source, discusses key takeaways with you, writes a summary page in the wiki, updates the index, updates relevant entity and concept pages across the wiki, and appends an entry to the log. A single source might touch 10-15 wiki pages. Personally I prefer to ingest sources one at a time and stay involved — I read the summaries, check the updates, and guide the LLM on what to emphasize. But you could also batch-ingest many sources at once with less supervision. It's up to you to develop the workflow that fits your style and document it in the schema for future sessions.

**Query.** You ask questions against the wiki. The LLM searches for relevant pages, reads them, and synthesizes an answer with citations. Answers can take different forms depending on the question — a markdown page, a comparison table, a slide deck (Marp), a chart (matplotlib), a canvas. The important insight: **good answers can be filed back into the wiki as new pages.** A comparison you asked for, an analysis, a connection you discovered — these are valuable and shouldn't disappear into chat history. This way your explorations compound in the knowledge base just like ingested sources do.

**Lint.** Periodically, ask the LLM to health-check the wiki. Look for: contradictions between pages, stale claims that newer sources have superseded, orphan pages with no inbound links, important concepts mentioned but lacking their own page, missing cross-references, data gaps that could be filled with a web search. The LLM is good at suggesting new questions to investigate and new sources to look for. This keeps the wiki healthy as it grows.

## Indexing and logging

Two special files help the LLM (and you) navigate the wiki as it grows. They serve different purposes:

**index.md** is content-oriented. It's a catalog of everything in the wiki — each page listed with a link, a one-line summary, and optionally metadata like date or source count. Organized by category (entities, concepts, sources, etc.). The LLM updates it on every ingest. When answering a query, the LLM reads the index first to find relevant pages, then drills into them. This works surprisingly well at moderate scale (~100 sources, ~hundreds of pages) and avoids the need for embedding-based RAG infrastructure.

**log.md** is chronological. It's an append-only record of what happened and when — ingests, queries, lint passes. A useful tip: if each entry starts with a consistent prefix (e.g. `## [2026-04-02] ingest | Article Title`), the log becomes parseable with simple unix tools — `grep "^## \[" log.md | tail -5` gives you the last 5 entries. The log gives you a timeline of the wiki's evolution and helps the LLM understand what's been done recently.

## Optional: CLI tools

At some point you may want to build small tools that help the LLM operate on the wiki more efficiently. A search engine over the wiki pages is the most obvious one — at small scale the index file is enough, but as the wiki grows you want proper search. [qmd](https://github.com/tobi/qmd) is a good option: it's a local search engine for markdown files with hybrid BM25/vector search and LLM re-ranking, all on-device. It has both a CLI (so the LLM can shell out to it) and an MCP server (so the LLM can use it as a native tool). You could also build something simpler yourself — the LLM can help you vibe-code a naive search script as the need arises.

## Tips and tricks

- **Obsidian Web Clipper** is a browser extension that converts web articles to markdown. Very useful for quickly getting sources into your raw collection.
- **Download images locally.** In Obsidian Settings → Files and links, set "Attachment folder path" to a fixed directory (e.g. `raw/assets/`). Then in Settings → Hotkeys, search for "Download" to find "Download attachments for current file" and bind it to a hotkey (e.g. Ctrl+Shift+D). After clipping an article, hit the hotkey and all images get downloaded to local disk. This is optional but useful — it lets the LLM view and reference images directly instead of relying on URLs that may break. Note that LLMs can't natively read markdown with inline images in one pass — the workaround is to have the LLM read the text first, then view some or all of the referenced images separately to gain additional context. It's a bit clunky but works well enough.
- **Obsidian's graph view** is the best way to see the shape of your wiki — what's connected to what, which pages are hubs, which are orphans.
- **Marp** is a markdown-based slide deck format. Obsidian has a plugin for it. Useful for generating presentations directly from wiki content.
- **Dataview** is an Obsidian plugin that runs queries over page frontmatter. If your LLM adds YAML frontmatter to wiki pages (tags, dates, source counts), Dataview can generate dynamic tables and lists.
- The wiki is just a git repo of markdown files. You get version history, branching, and collaboration for free.

## Why this works

The tedious part of maintaining a knowledge base is not the reading or the thinking — it's the bookkeeping. Updating cross-references, keeping summaries current, noting when new data contradicts old claims, maintaining consistency across dozens of pages. Humans abandon wikis because the maintenance burden grows faster than the value. LLMs don't get bored, don't forget to update a cross-reference, and can touch 15 files in one pass. The wiki stays maintained because the cost of maintenance is near zero.

The human's job is to curate sources, direct the analysis, ask good questions, and think about what it all means. The LLM's job is everything else.

The idea is related in spirit to Vannevar Bush's Memex (1945) — a personal, curated knowledge store with associative trails between documents. Bush's vision was closer to this than to what the web became: private, actively curated, with the connections between documents as valuable as the documents themselves. The part he couldn't solve was who does the maintenance. The LLM handles that.


## Note

This document is intentionally abstract. It describes the idea, not a specific implementation. The exact directory structure, the schema conventions, the page formats, the tooling — all of that will depend on your domain, your preferences, and your LLM of choice. Everything mentioned above is optional and modular — pick what's useful, ignore what isn't. For example: your sources might be text-only, so you don't need image handling at all. Your wiki might be small enough that the index file is all you need, no search engine required. You might not care about slide decks and just want markdown pages. You might want a completely different set of output formats. The right way to use this is to share it with your LLM agent and work together to instantiate a version that fits your needs. The document's only job is to communicate the pattern. Your LLM can figure out the rest.

108:     && rg -q '^created:' "$f" && rg -q '^updated:' "$f" \
109:     && rg -q '^sources:' "$f" && rg -q '^status:' "$f" || echo "MISSING FRONTMATTER KEY: $f"
110: done
111: ```
112: Also confirm `type` ∈ {entity, concept, comparison, summary, source-note} and `status` ∈ {draft, stable} per the Page format section.
113: 
114: **4. Contradictions** — pages must not contradict each other, nor contradict `wiki/framework/src-structure.md` or the actual `src/` tree. Reconcile any conflicting claims (differing paths, component lists, version facts) by re-reading `src-structure.md` and the live `src/` directory; record resolutions in `log.md` and fix the offending page. Note contradictions explicitly rather than silently overwriting (per Page format).
115: 
116: **5. Stale claims** — verify version/file assertions against the repo. Confirm these exist at the stated locations (paths relative to `wiki/`):
117: ```bash
118: test -f ../VERSION && echo "VERSION ok" || echo "MISSING: ../VERSION"
119: test -f ../package.json && echo "package.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../package.json"
120: test -f ../registry.json && echo "registry.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../registry.json"
121: test -f ../src/metadata.json && echo "src/metadata.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../src/metadata.json"
122: ```
123: Any page asserting a version, file, or path that does not match the live repo is stale and must be corrected.
124: 
125: **6. Secret scan** — WikiJanitor may `grep` *any* directory (its `grep` permission is intentionally broad) to detect leaked secrets — API keys, tokens, credentials — that have landed in normal files. Sensitive-file paths (`.env`, `.key`, `.secret`, `.pem`, `.crt`, `credentials*`) are denied under `grep`, so known-secret files are never opened; only leaks into ordinary files are surfaced. Flag leaks to SystemBuilder; never write secret values into wiki pages.
126: 
127: ### Audit capture (anyone)
128: Ad-hoc, low-friction. While working on anything, if you spot a flaw in the wiki, append a bullet to `AUDIT.md` and return to the task — do not fix it inline. The recommended bullet shape is encoded as a comment in `AUDIT.md` itself:
129: 
130:   <where>: <problem> → <fix>
131: 
132: - `<where>` — path (+ optional `:line`) within the wiki, or `wiki-wide`.
133: - `<problem>` — one-line statement of what is wrong.
134: - `<fix>` — the proposed correction. WikiJanitor verifies it before applying; it is **not** trusted blindly.
135: 
136: The file is a scratchpad: it holds only unprocessed bullets. No structure beyond the bullet list is required.
137: 
138: ### Audit drain (WikiJanitor — Step 0 of standalone Lint)
139: Runs as the first step of a **standalone Lint** invocation (by WikiLibrarian or SystemBuilder). It is **never** part of Ingest or its post-ingest lint. When `AUDIT.md` is empty this step is a no-op. For each bullet in `AUDIT.md` (drain ALL, no per-run cap):
140: 1. **Verify the problem** is real (against `src/` or `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`).
141: 2. **Verify the proposed fix** is correct (same sources). Never apply a fix that cannot be verified.
142: 3. If both verify → apply the fix to the target page, append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] audit | <title>` to `log.md`, and **delete the bullet**.
143: 4. If either fails to verify → **surface the item to SystemBuilder** (carry the bullet text), append a `log.md` audit line, and **delete the bullet** (the scratchpad stays clean; surfacing is the handoff).
144: WikiJanitor **never spawns ResearchAgent and performs no external research** during audit drain — unverifiable-with-local-sources items are surfaced to SystemBuilder, not investigated. Mechanical fixes only; if `src-structure.md` lacks the assertion needed to verify, surface rather than guess EDAC layout.
145: 
146: ### Cross-Reference Protocol
147: The wiki must be a navigable graph, not a set of standalone blobs. Every page is responsible for linking its related concepts inline so WikiLibrarian can traverse and Lint can verify.
148: 
149: - **Inline links are mandatory.** Whenever a page mentions a concept that has (or should have) its own wiki page, embed an inline markdown link in the prose — e.g. `the [permission model](./permission-model.md) governs access`. A trailing `## Related` section is a supplement only; it does **not** substitute for inline links. Inline links are grep-discoverable, which is what Lint checks (Check 2) and what lets WikiLibrarian walk the graph.
150: - **Back-links.** When page A links to page B, WikiJanitor also ensures B's `## Related` (and, where natural, B's prose) acknowledges A — unless B is a deliberate hub. This keeps the graph bidirectional.
151: - **Lint enforces** (Check 2): inline + `## Related` links resolve; no orphan page (zero inbound links); gap detection — a concept mentioned but lacking a page is a candidate for the ingest queue (fed to ResearchAgent / WikiLibrarian); bidirectional-consistency warning on asymmetry (asymmetry is allowed for hubs, so warn, don't fail).
152: - **Format.** Use relative markdown links to the target `.md` (`[label](./target.md)` or `[label](../dir/target.md)`). Keep the label human-readable; the link target is what Lint greps.
153: 
154: ## index.md format
155: Catalog of all pages, grouped by directory, each with a one-line summary and optional metadata (date, source count). Updated on every ingest. Example:
156: 
157: ```markdown
158: # Wiki Index
159: ## framework/
160: - [Layered Architecture](framework/layered-architecture.md) — the 6-layer model.
161: ## harness/
162: - [Permission Model](harness/permission-model.md) — frontmatter allow/deny/ask.
163: ```
164: 
165: ## log.md format
166: Append-only. Each entry begins with a consistent prefix so it is parseable:
167: `## [YYYY-MM-DD] <op> | <Title>` where `<op>` ∈ `init | research | ingest | query | lint`. Example:
168: `## [2026-07-29] init | Wiki scaffolding created`.
169: 
170: ## Workflow is branching
171: The research loop is not a fixed sequence. SystemBuilder may fan out multiple subagents in parallel (e.g. several ResearchAgents, several WikiLibrarians) and may spawn itself (configured `mode: all`). WikiJanitor's ingest runs only when new research was produced; if a query is answered from existing pages, no research/ingest occurs.

(End of file - total 171 lines)
</content>
```

## Finding
**Yes — SCHEMA.md has grown past its role.** It now carries two kinds of content that don't belong to a *schema* in EDAC's multi-agent context, and it duplicates the agent definitions.

## The tension worth naming
Karpathy's pattern *does* define the schema as including "what workflows to follow when ingesting… maintaining the wiki" (llm-wiki.md, *Architecture → The schema*). In that architecture the principled split is: **structure in SCHEMA, procedure in the agents.** The schema shouldn't re-specify how an agent behaves when the agent file is what actually runs.

Let me reconstruct the argument from first principles.

**The single-agent case (karpathy's pattern):**
- One LLM agent. One config file (the schema). The agent reads it at the start of every session (or it's in context).
- The schema serves as: (a) structural contract (what artifacts exist, their shapes), AND (b) procedural guidance (what workflows to follow).
- Why is co-locating structure + procedure sound HERE?
  1. **Single reader, single source of truth.** There's exactly one actor. The config file IS the agent's operating manual. There's no other place the procedure could live — the agent has no "definition file" separate from its system prompt. So putting procedure in the config is not duplication; it's the only copy.
  2. **No drift surface.** With one actor and one file, there's nothing to drift against. The "procedure" and the "structure" are consumed by the same context window in the same read. They can't contradict each other because they're literally adjacent in the same document the agent loads.
  3. **Context economy.** The agent needs both "what does the wiki look like" and "what do I do when a source arrives" in context to act. A single file delivers both in one load. Splitting would mean the agent must read two files, and the procedural file would have to be re-specified anyway (since the agent has no other home for it).
  4. **The schema IS the agent's constitution.** In single-agent, the schema plays the role that, in EDAC, is split between SCHEMA.md (contract) + agent definitions (constitution). There's no separate "agent definition" because the agent is generic (Codex/Claude/OpenCode Pi). So procedure must live in the schema — there's nowhere else.

So in single-agent: structure+procedure co-located is sound because (1) it's the only copy (no duplication possible), (2) one reader (no drift), (3) the agent has no alternative home for procedure.

**The multi-agent case (EDAC):**
- Multiple actors: SystemBuilder (primary) + ResearchAgent + WikiJanitor + WikiLibrarian subagents. Each subagent has its OWN definition file (`.opencode/agents/subagents/wiki-janitor.md` etc.) which IS its constitution/operating manual — loaded when that agent runs.
- The schema (SCHEMA.md) is a shared contract that all actors reference.

Why does co-locating procedure in SCHEMA become unsound HERE?

1. **Procedure now HAS a natural home: the agent definition.** Unlike the single-agent case, each subagent has a dedicated file that is loaded when it runs. That file is the rightful owner of "how this agent behaves" (Tier 1/2/3, rules, conflict_resolution). Putting the same procedure in SCHEMA creates a SECOND copy. In single-agent there was no second copy possible; in multi-agent there is, and that's the bug.

2. **Drift is now possible and likely.** Two (or more) files now state the same procedure: SCHEMA.md and wiki-janitor.md. They're edited by different workflows (I just edited both for audit). They will diverge. In single-agent, divergence was impossible (one file). In multi-agent, every procedure duplicated across schema+agent is a latent contradiction. The schema says "Lint does X"; the agent says "Lint does Y" — which wins? Ambiguity is a bug (per my own First Principles: "structure is an API contract — ambiguity is not a style choice but a bug").

3. **Authority ambiguity.** In EDAC, SCHEMA says "this file is the contract every wiki actor follows." But the agent definitions are what the harness actually loads and executes. If SCHEMA and the agent disagree, the agent's definition is what runs — so the agent definition is the de-facto source of truth, making SCHEMA's copy both redundant AND potentially misleading (a reader trusting SCHEMA gets stale info). The single-source-of-truth principle says: the executable artifact owns the procedure; the contract references it.

4. **Reader segmentation / context economy inverts.** In single-agent, one reader needed everything in one file. In multi-agent, DIFFERENT readers need DIFFERENT subsets:
   - SystemBuilder needs the contract (layout, formats, routing: who does what) to orchestrate.
   - WikiJanitor needs its own procedure (Tier 1/2/3) when it runs — and it gets that from its definition file, NOT from SCHEMA.md (SCHEMA is SystemBuilder's context, not necessarily loaded into the subagent).
   - So putting WikiJanitor's full Lint procedure in SCHEMA.md loads procedure into SystemBuilder's context (where it's not the executor) while the executor (WikiJanitor) loads it from its own file. That's misrouted context: the executor doesn't read SCHEMA for its procedure (it reads its definition), so SCHEMA's copy is dead weight for the executor and a drift risk for the orchestrator.
   - Actually, does WikiJanitor read SCHEMA.md? Its permission allows read wiki/**, and its rules reference src-structure.md. It may read SCHEMA for guidance. But its DEFINITION already encodes the procedure. So even if it reads both, the definition is authoritative. The duplication remains.

5. **The contract's job is different from the executor's job.** A contract specifies interfaces and invariants (what artifacts exist, their shapes, the routing). An executor specification specifies algorithms (how to lint, step by step). Mixing them in one file for multiple agents means the file tries to be both a shared interface doc AND N per-agent manuals. That's category confusion — the file loses a single clear purpose, which is exactly the "more than a schema should be" symptom the user spotted.

6. **Scaling.** As more agents are added (ResearchAgent, WikiLibrarian), each would contribute a procedure section to SCHEMA. SCHEMA would balloon into a multi-manual. The justification rests on one load-bearing fact: **whether procedure has an alternative home, and how many actors read the file.** That single fact flips the soundness.

## Single-agent: co-location is necessary *and* safe
In karpathy's pattern there is one LLM and one config file. The schema is the agent's entire operating manual.

1. **It's the only copy — duplication is impossible.** The agent has no separate "definition file"; its system prompt is generic (Codex/Claude/Pi). Procedure *must* live in the schema, because there is nowhere else for it to live. A second copy cannot exist, so drift cannot arise.
2. **One reader, one context load.** Structure and procedure are consumed by the same context window in the same read. They are literally adjacent; they cannot contradict each other.
3. **The schema *is* the agent's constitution.** There is no split between "contract" and "executor" because there is no executor distinct from the reader. So "structure + procedure in one file" isn't a category error — it's the only shape the document can take.
4. **Context economy favours one file.** The agent needs both "what does the wiki look like" and "what do I do when a source arrives" to act. One file delivers both in one load.

So in single-agent, co-location isn't a compromise — it's the only coherent design.

## Multi-agent: co-location becomes redundant *and* risky
EDAC has per-agent definition files (`.opencode/agents/subagents/wiki-janitor.md`, etc.) that are loaded and executed when each subagent runs. That changes the topology from 1-reader/1-file to N-readers/N-files. Procedure now has a natural home — and that's exactly why putting it in the shared schema turns unsound:

1. **Procedure has a home → a second copy is now a bug, not a necessity.** WikiJanitor's Tier 2 *is* its Lint procedure. SCHEMA.md repeating checks 1–6 is a redundant copy. In single-agent redundancy was impossible; here it's a latent contradiction.
2. **Drift is now possible and likely.** SCHEMA and `wiki-janitor.md` state the same procedure and are edited by different workflows (I just edited both for audit). They *will* diverge. Ambiguity between two statements of the same rule is a bug, not a style choice.
3. **Authority ambiguity.** SCHEMA says "the contract every actor follows," but the harness executes the *agent definition*. If they disagree, the definition wins — so SCHEMA's copy is both redundant and potentially *misleading* (a reader trusting SCHEMA gets stale info). Single-source-of-truth says: the executable artifact owns the procedure; the contract references it.
4. **Context is misrouted.** SystemBuilder reads SCHEMA; WikiJanitor reads its own definition when it runs. Putting WikiJanitor's Lint steps in SCHEMA loads procedure into the *orchestrator's* context (where it doesn't execute) while the *executor* loads it from its definition. The executor doesn't act from SCHEMA — so SCHEMA's copy is dead weight for it and a drift surface for the orchestrator.
5. **Category confusion.** A contract specifies interfaces and invariants (artifacts, shapes, routing). An executor spec specifies algorithms (step-by-step lint). One file trying to be both a shared interface *and* N per-agent manuals loses a single clear purpose — which is precisely the "more than a schema should be" symptom you spotted.
6. **Scaling is O(agents × procedure).** Each new agent (ResearchAgent, WikiLibrarian) would add a procedure section to SCHEMA. The single-agent schema stays small because there's one actor; the multi-agent schema-with-procedures balloons. Karpathy himself advocates modularity — procedure belongs in the module (the agent), not the shared contract.

## Why "agents own procedure" beats the inverse
One could argue: keep SCHEMA canonical for procedure, make agents thin pointers. That's *worse*, because the harness loads the **agent definition** as the executable artifact. The agent acts from its definition, not from SCHEMA (SCHEMA is SystemBuilder's context). For the agent to execute reliably, the procedure must be *in the loaded artifact*. "Schema canonical, agent fetches it at runtime" is fragile (depends on the agent remembering to read it, path resolution, context cost) and still leaves the procedure in two places. So the definition owns procedure; SCHEMA references it. That's the clean single-source-of-truth.

## Precise scope of the claim
The objection is to **detailed procedure duplication** (the `rg` commands, step-by-step drains), not to *naming* workflows in the schema. A one-line routing pointer — "Lint → WikiJanitor, Tier 2" — is correct and recommended; it's declarative structure, not a second manual. The unsound part is the *full procedure* living in both.

## The honest contingency
If EDAC were single-agent (one generic agent doing everything), my Option A would be *wrong* and karpathy's co-location would be right — because then procedure would have no alternative home. The recommendation is contingent on the multi-agent architecture, not a universal rule. The architecture is what flips the calculus.

So: co-location is sound when there's one reader and no other home for procedure; it becomes unsound the moment each actor gets its own executable definition file, because that file is the proper, non-redundant home for procedure.

**SystemBuilder** (`system-builder.md`) — treats SCHEMA as authoritative:
- L354: "`index.md` (catalog), `log.md` (append-only record), `TODO.md` (build plan), `SCHEMA.md` (governing contract)."
- L358: "Use the wiki *frequently*. Before asserting an EDAC convention, harness detail, or OAC-derived claim, consult `index.md` and read the relevant page; verify against the wiki instead of reconstructing from memory."

So SystemBuilder is instructed to consult the wiki and treat `SCHEMA.md` as the governing contract. ✅ That part of my claim holds.

**WikiJanitor** (`wiki-janitor.md`) — does **not** ignore SCHEMA; it explicitly defers to it:
- L98: "the `rg` / `test -f` commands in **SCHEMA's Lint procedure** are translated to `grep` / `glob` calls"
- L99: "run the three greps … (**mirroring SCHEMA's Lint procedure**)"

So WikiJanitor's own definition declares its Lint checks are a **translation/mirror of SCHEMA's Lint procedure**. The authority flows **SCHEMA → agent**, not agent → SCHEMA.

My justification for Option A rested on "WikiJanitor reads its own definition; SCHEMA merely references it." The file shows the opposite: WikiJanitor's procedure is *derived from* SCHEMA. So **SCHEMA is already the canonical procedure source**, and the agent is a translation layer. My recommendation to "move procedure into the agents and have SCHEMA reference them" was **backwards** — it would invert the authority direction that both the files and karpathy's pattern already establish.

- **In the agent files, replace the re-stated procedure bodies with references to SCHEMA's procedure sections** — e.g. WikiJanitor Tier 2 becomes "Execute SCHEMA.md §Lint checks 1–6, translating `rg`→`grep` / `test -f`→`glob`" — instead of re-listing the checks. One editable copy; the agent points to it.
- This removes the drift surface while preserving the SCHEMA→agent authority that the evidence confirms.

### Lint (WikiJanitor)
Standalone health-check of the generated pages. WikiJanitor verifies, against `src/` and `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`:
1. **OAC-path tyranny** — no generated page asserts an OAC `.opencode/` path or wrong `src/` path as EDAC fact.
2. **Structural-claim traceability** — every EDAC path/directory/layout assertion traces to `src-structure.md`.
3. **Cross-link integrity** — inline + `## Related` links resolve; no orphan pages; gap detection for concepts lacking a page.
4. **Frontmatter compliance** — all seven required keys present; `type`/`status` enums valid.
5. **Contradictions** — pages (and `src-structure.md` / live `src/`) do not contradict.
6. **Stale claims** — version/file/path assertions match the live repo.
7. **Secret scan** — leaked secrets in ordinary files are flagged (never written into pages).

Exempt from these checks: `sources/` (immutable upstream docs), `SCHEMA.md`, `TODO.md`, `log.md`, `AUDIT.md` (scratchpad), and `framework/src-structure.md` (legitimately quotes wrong forms to explain the fix).

Operational steps and tool translations: **WikiJanitor, Tier 2** (this schema is the canonical *what*; the agent file is the *how*).
```

### Audit drain (WikiJanitor — Step 0 of standalone Lint)
Runs as the first step of a **standalone Lint** invocation (by WikiLibrarian or SystemBuilder). It is **never** part of Ingest or its post-ingest lint. When `AUDIT.md` is empty this step is a no-op. For each bullet in `AUDIT.md` (drain ALL, no per-run cap):
1. **Verify the problem** is real (against `src/` or `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`).
2. **Verify the proposed fix** is correct (same sources). Never apply a fix that cannot be verified.
3. If both verify → apply the fix to the target page, append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] audit | <title>` to `log.md`, and **delete the bullet**.
4. If either fails to verify → **surface the item to SystemBuilder** (carry the bullet text), append a `log.md` audit line, and **delete the bullet** (the scratchpad stays clean; surfacing is the handoff).
WikiJanitor **never spawns ResearchAgent and performs no external research** during audit drain — unverifiable-with-local-sources items are surfaced to SystemBuilder, not investigated. Mechanical fixes only; if `src-structure.md` lacks the assertion needed to verify, surface rather than guess EDAC layout.
```

## Purpose
The wiki is a persistent, compounding knowledge base used while developing `src/`.
It is not a user-facing browse tool. The user interacts only with SystemBuilder;
subagents are spawned by SystemBuilder, never directly.

Pattern reference: `llm-wiki.md` (the abstract LLM-wiki idea this repo instantiates).

## Authority & layering
This file is the **canonical procedure source** for the EDAC wiki. It defines what the wiki is, its structure, and what workflows are performed — the contract every wiki actor follows.

The schema is **conceptual**: it says *what* to do. Agent definition files under `.opencode/agents/subagents/` (and the primary `system-builder.md`) encode the agent-specific operating procedures and protocols — they say *how* to do it. A schema statement and an agent definition must never disagree; if they appear to, SCHEMA is authoritative and the agent definition is corrected to mirror it.

Concretely:
- **SCHEMA.md** — structure, conventions, and the *what* of each workflow (Research, Ingest, Query, Lint, Audit). The single editable home for procedure intent.
- **Agent definitions** — the *how*: operational steps, tool translations, tiers, and conflict handling for the agent that owns each workflow.

## Layout
```

### Research (ResearchAgent)
```

Edit 3: Lint reframe. Old is lines 74-125 (from "### Lint (WikiJanitor)" through "never write secret values into wiki pages."). Let me capture exact text. From m0021:

```
### Lint (WikiJanitor)
Run after every ingest and on demand. Scope: only generated pages under `framework/`, `harness/`, `research/`. WikiJanitor may use **read-only** git (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git ls-files`, `git rev-parse`) to inspect repo state for verification, but never commits, pushes, or modifies the working tree.

> **`sources/` is immutable OAC raw documentation — never lint it for OAC paths; those are upstream documents, not EDAC assertions.** Correction/explanation contexts (`wiki/TODO.md`, `wiki/log.md`, `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`) are exempt from the OAC-path checks below because they deliberately quote the wrong forms to explain the fix. `wiki/AUDIT.md` is a scratchpad, not a generated page, and is exempt from **all** generated-page checks (OAC-path, frontmatter, cross-link, staleness): WikiJanitor drains and deletes its bullets, so it must never be linted as content.

**1. OAC-path tyranny** — no generated page may assert an OAC `.opencode/` path or a wrong `src/` path as EDAC fact. The greps below must return **zero matches** (Lint passes when grep fails). Run from `wiki/`:

```bash
# 1a. OAC metadata path must be src/metadata.json, never .opencode/config/agent-metadata.json
rg -n '\.opencode/config/agent-metadata\.json' framework harness research --glob '!framework/src-structure.md'

# 1b. bare/unqualified agent-metadata.json must be src/metadata.json
#     (src/metadata.json does NOT contain this substring, so a clean page yields no match)
rg -n 'agent-metadata\.json' framework harness research --glob '!framework/src-structure.md'

# 1c. registry.json lives at repo root, never under src/
rg -n 'src/registry\.json' framework harness research --glob '!framework/src-structure.md'
```

1d. **Structural-claim traceability** — every EDAC file path, directory, or layout assertion in a generated page must trace to `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`. For each path-like token a page asserts, confirm it appears in (or is consistent with) the tables in `src-structure.md`. If a claim cannot be traced, correct it against the live `src/` tree or flag it in `TODO.md`.

**2. Cross-link integrity**
- Every relative markdown link (`[text](path.md)`, `[text](../dir/page.md)`) must resolve to an existing file. Extract links, then verify each target exists relative to the referencing page:
  ```bash
  rg -no '\[[^\]]+\]\(([^)]+\.md)\)' framework harness research
  ```
  (Anchored links `path.md#sec` are rare here; re-check any that the pattern misses.)
- **Orphan pages** — flag any generated page with zero inbound links (no other page links to it). Cross-check against `index.md` and the link graph.
- **Missing pages** — flag concepts/entities named in pages (especially `tags`, `sources`, and "Related" sections) that are referenced but have no corresponding page.

**3. Frontmatter compliance** — every generated page must open with valid YAML frontmatter containing exactly these keys: `title`, `type`, `tags`, `created`, `updated`, `sources`, `status`. Verify:
```bash
for f in $(rg -l '^---$' framework harness research); do
  rg -q '^title:' "$f" && rg -q '^type:' "$f" && rg -q '^tags:' "$f" \
    && rg -q '^created:' "$f" && rg -q '^updated:' "$f" \
    && rg -q '^sources:' "$f" && rg -q '^status:' "$f" || echo "MISSING FRONTMATTER KEY: $f"
done
```
Also confirm `type` ∈ {entity, concept, comparison, summary, source-note} and `status` ∈ {draft, stable} per the Page format section.

**4. Contradictions** — pages must not contradict each other, nor contradict `wiki/framework/src-structure.md` or the actual `src/` tree. Reconcile any conflicting claims (differing paths, component lists, version facts) by re-reading `src-structure.md` and the live `src/` directory; record resolutions in `log.md` and fix the offending page. Note contradictions explicitly rather than silently overwriting (per Page format).

**5. Stale claims** — verify version/file assertions against the repo. Confirm these exist at the stated locations (paths relative to `wiki/`):
```bash
test -f ../VERSION && echo "VERSION ok" || echo "MISSING: ../VERSION"
test -f ../package.json && echo "package.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../package.json"
test -f ../registry.json && echo "registry.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../registry.json"
test -f ../src/metadata.json && echo "src/metadata.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../src/metadata.json"
```
Any page asserting a version, file, or path that does not match the live repo is stale and must be corrected.

**6. Secret scan** — WikiJanitor may `grep` *any* directory (its `grep` permission is intentionally broad) to detect leaked secrets — API keys, tokens, credentials — that have landed in normal files. Sensitive-file paths (`.env`, `.key`, `.secret`, `.pem`, `.crt`, `credentials*`) are denied under `grep`, so known-secret files are never opened; only leaks into ordinary files are surfaced. Flag leaks to SystemBuilder; never write secret values into wiki pages.
```

### Lint (WikiJanitor)
Standalone health-check of the generated pages (`framework/`, `harness/`, `research/`). WikiJanitor verifies, against `src/` and `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`:
1. **OAC-path tyranny** — no generated page asserts an OAC `.opencode/` path or a wrong `src/` path as EDAC fact.
2. **Structural-claim traceability** — every EDAC path/directory/layout assertion traces to `src-structure.md`.
3. **Cross-link integrity** — inline + `## Related` links resolve; no orphan pages; gap detection for concepts lacking a page.
4. **Frontmatter compliance** — all seven required keys present; `type`/`status` enums valid.
5. **Contradictions** — pages (and `src-structure.md` / live `src/`) do not contradict.
6. **Stale claims** — version/file/path assertions match the live repo.
7. **Secret scan** — leaked secrets in ordinary files are flagged (never written into pages).

Exempt from these checks: `sources/` (immutable upstream docs), `SCHEMA.md`, `TODO.md`, `log.md`, `AUDIT.md` (scratchpad), and `framework/src-structure.md` (legitimately quotes wrong forms to explain the fix).

Operational steps and tool translations: **WikiJanitor, Tier 2** — this schema is the canonical *what*; the agent file is the *how*.

Edit 4: Audit drain reframe. Old (lines 138-144):
```
### Audit drain (WikiJanitor — Step 0 of standalone Lint)
Runs as the first step of a **standalone Lint** invocation (by WikiLibrarian or SystemBuilder). It is **never** part of Ingest or its post-ingest lint. When `AUDIT.md` is empty this step is a no-op. For each bullet in `AUDIT.md` (drain ALL, no per-run cap):
1. **Verify the problem** is real (against `src/` or `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`).
2. **Verify the proposed fix** is correct (same sources). Never apply a fix that cannot be verified.
3. If both verify → apply the fix to the target page, append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] audit | <title>` to `log.md`, and **delete the bullet**.
4. If either fails to verify → **surface the item to SystemBuilder** (carry the bullet text), append a `log.md` audit line, and **delete the bullet** (the scratchpad stays clean; surfacing is the handoff).
WikiJanitor **never spawns ResearchAgent and performs no external research** during audit drain — unverifiable-with-local-sources items are surfaced to SystemBuilder, not investigated. Mechanical fixes only; if `src-structure.md` lacks the assertion needed to verify, surface rather than guess EDAC layout.
```
New:
```
### Audit drain (WikiJanitor — Step 0 of standalone Lint)
A standalone Lint begins by draining `AUDIT.md`: for each bullet, WikiJanitor **verifies the problem and the proposed fix** against `src/` or `src-structure.md`; if both verify it applies the fix, logs it, and deletes the bullet; if either fails it **surfaces the item to SystemBuilder** and deletes the bullet. It never spawns ResearchAgent or does external research. When `AUDIT.md` is empty this step is a no-op.

Operational steps: **WikiJanitor, Tier 2, Step 0** — schema = *what*; agent = *how*.
```

### Lint (WikiJanitor)
Run after every ingest and on demand. Scope: only generated pages under `framework/`, `harness/`, `research/`. WikiJanitor may use **read-only** git (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git ls-files`, `git rev-parse`) to inspect repo state for verification, but never commits, pushes, or modifies the working tree.

> **`sources/` is immutable OAC raw documentation — never lint it for OAC paths; those are upstream documents, not EDAC assertions.** Correction/explanation contexts (`wiki/TODO.md`, `wiki/log.md`, `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`) are exempt from the OAC-path checks below because they deliberately quote the wrong forms to explain the fix. `wiki/AUDIT.md` is a scratchpad, not a generated page, and is exempt from **all** generated-page checks (OAC-path, frontmatter, cross-link, staleness): WikiJanitor drains and deletes its bullets, so it must never be linted as content.

**1. OAC-path tyranny** — no generated page may assert an OAC `.opencode/` path or a wrong `src/` path as EDAC fact. The greps below must return **zero matches** (Lint passes when grep fails). Run from `wiki/`:

```bash
# 1a. OAC metadata path must be src/metadata.json, never .opencode/config/agent-metadata.json
rg -n '\.opencode/config/agent-metadata\.json' framework harness research --glob '!framework/src-structure.md'

# 1b. bare/unqualified agent-metadata.json must be src/metadata.json
#     (src/metadata.json does NOT contain this substring, so a clean page yields no match)
rg -n 'agent-metadata\.json' framework harness research --glob '!framework/src-structure.md'

# 1c. registry.json lives at repo root, never under src/
rg -n 'src/registry\.json' framework harness research --glob '!framework/src-structure.md'
```

1d. **Structural-claim traceability** — every EDAC file path, directory, or layout assertion in a generated page must trace to `wiki/framework/src-structure.md`. For each path-like token a page asserts, confirm it appears in (or is consistent with) the tables in `src-structure.md`. If a claim cannot be traced, correct it against the live `src/` tree or flag it in `TODO.md`.

**2. Cross-link integrity**
- Every relative markdown link (`[text](path.md)`, `[text](../dir/page.md)`) must resolve to an existing file. Extract links, then verify each target exists relative to the referencing page:
  ```bash
  rg -no '\[[^\]]+\]\(([^)]+\.md)\)' framework harness research
  ```
  (Anchored links `path.md#sec` are rare here; re-check any that the pattern misses.)
- **Orphan pages** — flag any generated page with zero inbound links (no other page links to it). Cross-check against `index.md` and the link graph.
- **Missing pages** — flag concepts/entities named in pages (especially `tags`, `sources`, and "Related" sections) that are referenced but have no corresponding page.

**3. Frontmatter compliance** — every generated page must open with valid YAML frontmatter containing exactly these keys: `title`, `type`, `tags`, `created`, `updated`, `sources`, `status`. Verify:
```bash
for f in $(rg -l '^---$' framework harness research); do
  rg -q '^title:' "$f" && rg -q '^type:' "$f" && rg -q '^tags:' "$f" \
    && rg -q '^created:' "$f" && rg -q '^updated:' "$f" \
    && rg -q '^sources:' "$f" && rg -q '^status:' "$f" || echo "MISSING FRONTMATTER KEY: $f"
done
```
Also confirm `type` ∈ {entity, concept, comparison, summary, source-note} and `status` ∈ {draft, stable} per the Page format section.

**4. Contradictions** — pages must not contradict each other, nor contradict `wiki/framework/src-structure.md` or the actual `src/` tree. Reconcile any conflicting claims (differing paths, component lists, version facts) by re-reading `src-structure.md` and the live `src/` directory; record resolutions in `log.md` and fix the offending page. Note contradictions explicitly rather than silently overwriting (per Page format).

**5. Stale claims** — verify version/file assertions against the repo. Confirm these exist at the stated locations (paths relative to `wiki/`):
```bash
test -f ../VERSION && echo "VERSION ok" || echo "MISSING: ../VERSION"
test -f ../package.json && echo "package.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../package.json"
test -f ../registry.json && echo "registry.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../registry.json"
test -f ../src/metadata.json && echo "src/metadata.json ok" || echo "MISSING: ../src/metadata.json"
```
Any page asserting a version, file, or path that does not match the live repo is stale and must be corrected.

**6. Secret scan** — WikiJanitor may `grep` *any* directory (its `grep` permission is intentionally broad) to detect leaked secrets — API keys, tokens, credentials — that have landed in normal files. Sensitive-file paths (`.env`, `.key`, `.secret`, `.pem`, `.crt`, `credentials*`) are denied under `grep`, so known-secret files are never opened; only leaks into ordinary files are surfaced. Flag leaks to SystemBuilder; never write secret values into wiki pages.
```

22: ## Authority & layering
23: This file is the **canonical procedure source** for the EDAC wiki. It defines what the wiki is, its structure, and what workflows are performed — the contract every wiki actor follows.

29: - **The agents** (ResearchAgent, WikiJanitor, WikiLibrarian, SystemBuilder) — the *how*: operational steps, tool translations, and conflict handling for the agent that owns each workflow.
30: 
31: ## Layout
32: - `sources/` — raw, immutable primary data. ResearchAgent writes cited research docs here; the user may also drop sources. Never modified after creation.
33: - `framework/` — generated pages on EDAC's conceptual architecture (agentic-system design, the layered model, registry/install model, component taxonomy).
34: - `harness/` — generated pages on OpenCode harness specifics (agent frontmatter, permission model, tools, MCP, subagent spawning, context/`compress`).
35: - `research/` — generated pages on external references, findings, comparisons (OpenAgentsControl lineage, upstream OpenCode docs, related projects).

38: - `log.md` — chronological activity record (append-only).

114: 
115: ### Cross-Reference Protocol
116: The wiki is a navigable graph, not standalone blobs. These are conventions (the *what*); WikiJanitor enforces them in Lint and WikiLibrarian traverses them in Query. Every page is responsible for linking its related concepts inline so WikiLibrarian can traverse and Lint can verify.
117: 
118: - **Inline links are mandatory.** Whenever a page mentions a concept that has (or should have) its own wiki page, embed an inline markdown link in the prose — e.g. `the [permission model](./permission-model.md) governs access`. A trailing `## Related` section is a supplement only; it does **not** substitute for inline links. Inline links are grep-discoverable, which is what Lint checks (Check 2) and what lets WikiLibrarian walk the graph.
119: - **Back-links.** When page A links to page B, WikiJanitor also ensures B's `## Related` (and, where natural, B's prose) acknowledges A — unless B is a deliberate hub. This keeps the graph bidirectional.
120: - **Lint enforces** (Check 2): inline + `## Related` links resolve; no orphan page (zero inbound links); gap detection — a concept mentioned but lacking a page is a candidate for the ingest queue (fed to ResearchAgent / WikiLibrarian); bidirectional-consistency warning on asymmetry (asymmetry is allowed for hubs, so warn, don't fail).
121: - **Format.** Use relative markdown links to the target `.md` (`[label](./target.md)` or `[label](../dir/target.md)`). Keep the label human-readable; the link target is what Lint greps.

112: ## Workflow
113: Ingest and Lint are separate invocations. Ingest always ends with a post-ingest lint of changed pages, and **never drains `AUDIT.md`**. 57: # WikiJanitor
58: > **Mission**: Distil verified, cross-linked knowledge into the EDAC wiki and keep it structurally honest — never asserting OAC packaging as EDAC fact.
59: > **Procedure authority**: The wiki's procedures (*what*) live in `wiki/SCHEMA.md` — the canonical, authoritative source. This file is the *how*: tool translations, tiers, and conflict handling. On any apparent conflict, SCHEMA wins and this file is corrected.
60: 
61: <rule id="oac_lineage_not_fact">OAC paths and structures are lineage, not EDAC fact. When a source describes OpenAgentsControl's layout (`.opencode/config/agent-metadata.json`, bare `agent-metadata.json`, `src/registry.json`, a `VERSION`-file claim), correct EDAC paths to the real layout in [src-structure.md](wiki/framework/src-structure.md). Never present an OAC path as EDAC's actual file.</rule>
62: 
63: <rule id="wiki_scope_only">You may only `edit` files under `wiki/**`. You never modify `src/` or any packaging file. Reading `src/**` is allowed for verification only. Versioning is SystemBuilder's authority: you never `git commit`, `git push`, `git add`, or otherwise modify the working tree — but you may run **read-only** git commands (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git ls-files`, `git rev-parse`) to inspect repo state for lint/verification.</rule>
64: 
65: <rule id="inline_crossref">Every related concept you mention in prose must carry an inline link to its wiki page (e.g. `[permission model](./permission-model.md)`) — per SCHEMA's Cross-Reference Protocol. A trailing `## Related` section is a supplement, not a substitute. Links must be grep-discoverable so WikiLibrarian can traverse the graph.</rule>
66: 
67: <rule id="auto_fix_mechanical">Auto-fix mechanical issues: OAC-path tyranny corrections, frontmatter gaps, broken links, and contradictions verifiable against `wiki/framework/src-structure.md` or the live `src/` tree (correct the page and record the resolution in `log.md`). Escalate only contradictions that cannot be verified against `src/` or `src-structure.md` to SystemBuilder; never silently resolve those.</rule>
68: 
69: <rule id="secret_scan">Your `grep` permission is intentionally broad (any directory) so you can scan for leaked secrets — API keys, tokens, credentials — across the repo, including outside `wiki/`. Sensitive-file paths (`.env`, `.key`, `.secret`, `.pem`, `.crt`, `credentials*`) are denied under `grep` so you never surface the contents of known-secret files; you only detect secrets that have leaked into normal files. Flag leaks; never print secret values into the wiki.</rule>
70:

74:   <system>Content-operations layer for the EDAC wiki; the shared service ResearchAgent and WikiLibrarian depend on.</system>
75:   <domain>Wiki ingestion, linting, cross-referencing, OAC-vs-EDAC path hygiene.</domain>
76:   <task>Ingest sources into well-formed pages; lint the wiki for tyranny, cross-reference integrity, and staleness.</task>
77:   <constraints>Write only to `wiki/`; no bash except read-only git inspection (`git status`/`log`/`diff`/`show`/`ls-files`/`rev-parse`); no git writes; no spawning other agents; inline cross-references mandatory.</constraints>
78: </context>
